title: Ash Wednesday
subtitle: New Orleans, Six Days of Carnival, February to March 1946

listing.title: Ash Wednesday 🎭
listing.blurb: New Orleans, 1946, the first Mardi Gras since the war. The man who filled the pay envelopes at a canal-side shipyard is pulled out of the Industrial Canal with whisky on his coat and none in him, and the police have already called it an accident. Follow a padded Navy contract from the back door of the morgue to two pay windows, a float lit by flambeaux and a masked ball, to noon on Ash Wednesday, when the books close for good. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: New Orleans in the spring of 1946 is a city of half a million people waking up from a war that made it rich. Its shipyards on the Industrial Canal built landing craft, tugs, lighters and Liberty ships by the hundred; now the Navy contracts are finished, the yards are laying men off by the thousand, and the veterans are home and looking for work. And for the first time since 1941 there will be Carnival: the old-line krewes are parading again, the floats are being built in borrowed warehouses, and on Tuesday 5 March, Mardi Gras, the whole city will put on a mask. At dawn on Friday 1 March the lock tender at the Industrial Canal pulls a body off the lock gates: Marcel Fontenot, forty-one, pay clerk at Ste. Claire Marine Ways, smelling of rye. By noon Captain Achille Lebeau of the 5th District has called it an accidental drowning of an intoxicated man, and the deputy coroner has signed it without opening the body. Marcel Fontenot did not drink. He was dead before he went into the water. And on the Wednesday before he died he took from the yard's pay vault the Navy copies of three years of pay summaries, which prove that Ste. Claire Marine Ways padded its cost-plus Navy contracts in two ways: it billed the Navy at the first-class welder's rate of $1.20 an hour for a hundred and forty Black welders it paid as helpers at seventy-eight cents, and it billed for a hundred and forty more men, 'colored labor gang No. 9', who never existed. More than a million dollars. At noon on Ash Wednesday, a young Navy auditor will sign a final settlement that closes the contracts for good, and on Thursday the yard will be sold to a Chicago company. Over six days of Carnival the party follows the case from the lock and the back door of the parish morgue to the Seventh Ward hall where sixty-one laid-off Black welders have kept every pay envelope for three years; into the shipyard, where the floats of the Krewe of Oneiros are being built in the mold loft over the pay vault; onto the parade route on Mardi Gras night, where the proof is hidden in a papier-mâché sea serpent rolling down St. Charles Avenue by flambeau light, with the killer riding on it in a mask; into a whites-only ball where the yard owner's granddaughter is Queen of Carnival; and to noon on Ash Wednesday, when the party must decide who the proof is for: the Navy, which wants its money back; the welders, who want their wages; the city, which wants its Carnival; or the dead man's widow, who wants his name.
hook: New Orleans, Friday 1 March 1946. Four days to Mardi Gras. The first Carnival since the war, and the city is already half in costume: crepe paper on the balconies of Royal Street, the krewes' colors in the shop windows on Canal, sailors and soldiers in uniform everywhere looking for a party or a job. It rained in the night and the streets steam. At a quarter to six this morning, the lock tender at the river end of the Industrial Canal saw something against the lock gates in the brown water, and it was a man in a grey suit, face down, with his shoes still tied. By eight o'clock the 5th District had a name, Marcel Fontenot, pay clerk at Ste. Claire Marine Ways, and by noon the 5th District had a verdict: drunk, fell in, drowned, a shame. His widow does not believe it, because her husband had not taken a drink in fifteen years. The detective who caught the case does not believe it, because his captain decided before the coroner did. A pay clerk's death is not news in Carnival week. But some people in this city are taking a great deal of trouble over it, and they are about to start taking trouble over you.

setting.name: New Orleans, Louisiana, Thursday 28 February to Ash Wednesday 6 March 1946
setting.description: The city is real, and so are the year, the Industrial Canal and its lock, the wartime shipbuilding boom and bust, Carnival's return in 1946 after four years without parades, the flambeaux, segregation law, the Fair Employment Practice Committee (dying for lack of funds) and the hard postwar fight by Black veterans to register and vote. Ste. Claire Marine Ways, the Krewe of Oneiros, the Crescent Statesman and every person in the story are invented. New Orleans in 1946 sits in a crescent bend of the Mississippi, below the river's level, behind levees, with Lake Pontchartrain to the north. Canal Street, the widest main street in America, divides the old Creole city downriver (the French Quarter, Esplanade Avenue, the Faubourg Marigny, the Seventh Ward, Tremé) from the American city upriver (the business district, St. Charles Avenue, the Garden District). Downriver past the Quarter are the Bywater and the Ninth Ward, and through the Ninth Ward runs the Industrial Canal, five miles of deep water cut in 1923 from the river to the lake, lined with shipyards that built for the Navy through the war. Ste. Claire Marine Ways is a mid-sized yard on the east bank, off Jourdan Avenue, founded by Honoré Ste. Claire in 1911: three building ways, a fitting-out pier, a mold loft and two pay windows. The city is segregated by law: streetcars carry a movable screen marked FOR COLORED PATRONS ONLY, cabs are licensed by race, hospitals, schools, bars and the ball of every old-line krewe are separate or closed. And the city is not two cities but many: white Creole families on Esplanade Avenue who have been here since the Spanish, Creoles of color in the Seventh Ward who have been here as long and are plasterers, cigar-makers, carpenters and doctors, American money on St. Charles Avenue, Irish and German families in the Channel, Sicilian families in the lower Quarter, Black working families in Tremé, Central City and the Ninth Ward, and seventy thousand returning veterans of every kind. They live closer together than the law pretends, and they know each other better than the law would like.
setting.atmosphere: Damp heat even in March, the river smell and coffee from the roasters on the riverfront, chicory and fried oysters and diesel. Brass bands practicing in the back of every hall for Carnival, and children's chalk on the banquettes. Rain that comes in fast off the lake in the afternoon and leaves the streets steaming. Purple, green and gold bunting. Ship horns on the canal at night and the clank of the lock. Neon on Canal Street and gas lamps on Esplanade. The tone is hard-boiled paperback: rye, cigarette smoke, sweat through a good shirt, a bruise, blood on a wharf plank, a man who lies to you politely in a beautiful room. Carnival should feel like what it is in 1946: a city exhaling after a war, joyful, loud, extravagant and real, and also a pageant of who rules whom, in which the men who own the city ride masked on floats and the Black men who carry their torches catch the coins thrown at their feet. Let both be true at once. Never use Black or Creole New Orleans as color or mystery: the people of the Seventh Ward are welders, doctors, cabdrivers, reporters and grandmothers with their own plans, and the color line is something the city does to them, which the GM should show plainly and never make picturesque.

regions.name: The Industrial Canal and the Ninth Ward
regions.description: Five miles of deep water from the Mississippi to Lake Pontchartrain, cut through the Ninth Ward in 1923. At the river end is the lock, with its tender's house and the St. Claude Avenue bridge over it; north of that, the Florida Avenue crossing and the shipyards. Ste. Claire Marine Ways is on the east bank off Jourdan Avenue in the Lower Ninth: a fence, a gatehouse with a night-pass log, two pay windows on the end of the office building (one painted WHITE, one painted COLORED, with separate lines in the yard), three building ways now mostly empty, a fitting-out pier with a crane, and the mold loft, a huge timber-floored shed where ship patterns were laid out full-size and where, this winter, the floats of the Krewe of Oneiros are being built. West of the canal, in the Upper Ninth and the Bywater, are the shotgun doubles of the yard's white workers, including the Fontenots' on Louisa Street; east of it, in the Lower Ninth, many of its Black workers' homes. The 5th District station house, Captain Lebeau's, is a brick building on the near side of the ward, ten minutes from the yard.

regions.name: The Seventh Ward and Tremé
regions.description: The old Creole downtown behind the French Quarter, north of Esplanade toward the lake: Creole cottages and shotguns with louvered shutters, corner groceries, benevolent association halls, the Tremé Taxi Company's stand, Anatole Pichon's plaster shop on Annette Street, the Crescent Statesman's office and press on North Claiborne Avenue, and the hall of the Equity Benevolent Association on North Roman Street, where Theo Dorsainville's sixty-one welders meet. Craftsmen, teachers, porters, longshoremen, insurance men, priests, doctors, numbers runners and nurses, Creoles of color and Black families from upriver, people who have lived under Jim Crow for fifty years and built a city of their own inside it. The white police come here to make arrests and not to answer calls. The Municipal Auditorium stands at the edge of Tremé, and it is where the white krewes hold their balls.

regions.name: Downtown and Canal Street
regions.description: The French Quarter's balconies and bars, Bourbon Street's clubs (the Café Isabeau, Solange Delery's room), Royal Street's antique shops, and Canal Street: department stores, movie palaces, the U.S. Custom House at the river end (the Navy's cost office is on its third floor), Terminal Station at the lake end where the Southern Railway's Crescent Limited leaves for New York, and between them the widest street in America, which on Mardi Gras night is packed from building to building. Upriver of Canal, the business district: Carondelet Street's offices (Prosper Vidrine's law firm, the Oneiros club rooms, Crescent Photostat Co.), Baronne Street's Hotel Vauclain, Lafayette Square and City Hall. The Criminal Courts Building at Tulane Avenue and Broad Street holds the courts, the parish prison behind it and, in its basement, the coroner's office and the parish morgue.

regions.name: Esplanade Avenue and St. Charles Avenue
regions.description: The two avenues of old money. Esplanade runs from the river to Bayou St. John under live oaks, the boulevard of the old French and Spanish families: the Ste. Claire house is here, a raised Italianate villa of 1858 with a carriage gate, a courtyard with a cistern, Honoré's library and the telephone in it, and so is the Lamarque house. St. Charles Avenue runs uptown under oaks too, with the streetcar on its neutral ground and the American money's mansions on either side, and on Mardi Gras night it is the route of the parades from Lee Circle down to Canal Street, lined twenty deep.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: The party has one Heat score for New Orleans, 0 to 10, tracked openly by the GM and announced whenever it changes. It starts at 0. It rises by 1 for being seen somewhere you should not be (the yard after dark, the krewe's den, the coroner's back door), leaning on the wrong man (a Ste. Claire, Captain Lebeau, Emile Gravier, Commander Pruett), a public fistfight or a story with your names in it; by 2 for gunfire, a car chase the police see, or breaking into a building; by 3 for a body. It falls by 1 for each half-day spent quietly. On Mardi Gras day, Heat does not rise for anything done in a mask that nobody sees under. At Heat 3 the cops start asking: Captain Lebeau's men tail the party and Det. Lamarque is ordered off the case. At Heat 6 someone is told to take care of you: Gravier sends men, the agency office is searched, and Lebeau has a pretext arrest ready. At Heat 9 the city is closed to you: licences pulled, a warrant on a charge, and nobody on Esplanade Avenue or at the 5th District will take your call. The GM should show plainly that the city does not spend Heat evenly: when it rises, the police pick up the Black characters' friends and kin first, and stop colored cabs on the St. Claude bridge. That is the injustice of the city, shown in the story. It is never a modifier on a player's roll.

campaignRules.name: Carnival Calendar
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on six fixed days and the opposition acts on them whether or not the party is watching. The unit of time is the scene, about two hours. cs-scenario-001 is Friday 1 and Saturday 2 March; cs-scenario-002 is Sunday 3 and Lundi Gras, Monday 4 March; cs-scenario-003 is Mardi Gras, Tuesday 5 March; cs-scenario-004 is Ash Wednesday, 6 March. If the party does not interfere, this happens. FRIDAY: body at the lock at 5:45 a.m.; Honoré Ste. Claire telephones Captain Lebeau at 6:10; Clovis Pinac moves Marcel's car out of the yard at 6:30; ruled accidental by noon; Emile Gravier's men search the Fontenot house at 11 p.m. SATURDAY: the body is released to Irene Fontenot for burial Monday; lawyer Prosper Vidrine offers the party $500 for 'company records'. SUNDAY: Gravier's men watch the Equity Benevolent Association hall. LUNDI GRAS: Lt. Whitcombe's walk-through of the yard at 10 a.m. with Commander Pruett; at 6 p.m. Lebeau has Marcel's notebook taken from the property room; at 10 p.m. Gravier's men set fire to the hall on North Roman Street to burn the pay envelopes. MARDI GRAS: the city is closed (courts, banks and the post office shut); the Krewe of Oneiros rolls at 6:30 p.m.; Pruett, masked on float fourteen, takes Marcel's packet from the Leviathan during the halt on Canal Street and burns it in a flambeau; ball at 9 p.m.; police sweep Canal Street at midnight. ASH WEDNESDAY: Theo Dorsainville arrested at 7 a.m. on a pretext; Pruett collects $50,000 from Lucien for the photostats at 10; Whitcombe signs the settlement at noon; Pruett leaves on the 1:15 p.m. Crescent Limited. THURSDAY: the yard is sold.

campaignRules.name: Three-Clue Rule
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the party must reach has at least three clues, in different places, and each scenario names them in its conclusions list. Core clues are found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with a relevant skill, or who asks the right person in a way that person will answer. Rolls add detail, speed or a bonus clue; a failed roll never hides a core clue. Where a clue sits behind the color line (a witness who will only talk to someone they trust, a place one character cannot enter), there is always another route to the same conclusion, and the GM should make the route through the Seventh Ward as rich as the route through Esplanade Avenue. When the table is stuck, use the case board (investigation.json the_case_board) or let a companion sum up what they know.

campaignRules.name: The Color Line
campaignRules.description: New Orleans in 1946 is a Jim Crow city by law, and this campaign treats segregation as what it was: an injustice enforced by police, courts, employers and custom, and fought every day by the people it was done to. It is never scenery and never a joke. It shapes the case: the padding worked because nobody at the Navy looked at the Black welders' pay, and the coroner signs Black deaths unseen. It shapes access: the Oneiros ball admits white guests only, the colored cab may legally carry only Black fares, a Black man may not sit in the Custom House waiting room with white men, and the 5th District arrests Black veterans for walking home. And it cuts both ways for access: the Seventh Ward, the Statesman, the Equity hall, Flint-Goodridge Hospital, the morgue porters and the flambeaux carriers will tell a Black or Creole character what they would never tell a white detective. No character's dice are ever penalised for race. The GM plays the city's people who enforce the line as antagonists and the people who live under it as full people with their own plans, never as helpers to white heroes. A player may always choose not to play a scene of humiliation; the GM then says it happened and moves on.

campaignRules.name: Masking Day
campaignRules.description: On Mardi Gras, and only on Mardi Gras, masking in the street is legal in New Orleans, and much of the city is in costume from dawn. Anyone masked is anonymous to anyone who does not know them well: recognising a masked person you know takes a DC 15 Insight or Perception check (advantage if you know their walk, voice or hands). The riders on the floats of the Krewe of Oneiros are masked and robed, nine to a float, and their identities are the krewe's oldest secret; the captain is unknown even to most members. Masks come off at midnight, when the police sweep Canal Street and Carnival ends. A party member in a mask on Mardi Gras day does not raise Heat for being seen (see Heat), but a mask is no help once you have been searched, cuffed or shot at.

campaignRules.name: Wages and Favors
campaignRules.description: Prices in 1946 dollars (investigation.json bribes_and_favors): a doorman or a streetcar conductor $1, a desk sergeant $10, a gate watchman $5, a look at the coroner's file $25, a seat on a Canal Street balcony on Mardi Gras night $5, a costume $3, a lawyer for a man arrested on a pretext $50, a bail bond for 'vagrancy' $25. The numbers that matter: a first-class welder's wage $1.20 an hour; a helper's 78 cents; the spread on all of Ste. Claire's Black welders across three years about $430,000, of which the sixty-one with envelopes are owed about $187,000; the ghost gang about $640,000; the Navy's draft settlement $38,000. Favors work as in the Fixer class, and Theo Dorsainville's favors come from the Seventh Ward, not from City Hall.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of New Orleans: the river along the bottom, the lake off the top, the Industrial Canal and the shipyards to the right, the Seventh Ward and Esplanade Avenue in the middle, Canal Street and the business district below them, St. Charles Avenue and the parade route to the left. The unit of time is the scene, about two hours, and the Carnival Calendar (see campaignRules) runs whether the party is watching or not. The party moves by car (Zélie Pichon's Duchess, if she is played, is the party's car), streetcar (the screen moves and the conductor enforces it), cab (licensed by race: a white cab will not take Black fares, and Duchess may legally carry only Black passengers, a law Zélie breaks with care), and on foot. From the Quarter to the canal is twenty minutes by car; to Esplanade Avenue ten; to the Criminal Courts fifteen. On Mardi Gras day nothing on wheels crosses St. Charles or Canal after noon, the courts, banks and post office are closed, and every street downtown is a crowd. The St. Claude Avenue bridge over the lock is the only quick way between the Quarter and the yard, and it lifts for ships without warning. The GM should make the city's geography matter: who can get into which room, how long it takes to cross town in Carnival traffic, and which neighbourhoods will hide whom.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. It does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Ste. Claire Marine Ways, the Krewe of Oneiros, the Equity Benevolent Association, the Crescent Statesman, the Café Isabeau, the Hotel Vauclain and every named person are fictional. The city, the Industrial Canal and its lock, the wartime shipbuilding boom, the 1946 return of Carnival, the flambeaux, the Navy's cost-plus contracts and final settlements, the Fair Employment Practice Committee, segregation law and the postwar voter registration drives of Black veterans are real history. No real private individual appears, and no real company is accused of anything.
controlFile.theTruth: From 1942 to 1945 Ste. Claire Marine Ways built steel lighters and harbor tugs for the Navy under three cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts: the Navy paid the yard's costs plus a fixed fee, so every dollar of cost the yard claimed was a dollar of Navy money. The yard padded the costs in two ways. The first was Honoré Ste. Claire's: from 1942 the yard hired about a hundred and forty Black welders, who did first-class work passed by the Navy's own inspectors, classified them as helpers, paid them seventy-eight cents an hour, and billed the Navy for them as Welders First Class at $1.20. Honoré calls this 'the custom of the river' and does not think of it as theft; it came to about $430,000. The second was Lucien Ste. Claire's: from 1943, with the stevedore contractor Emile Gravier and the Navy's resident inspector, Commander Thaddeus Pruett, Lucien carried a hundred and forty men on the payroll as 'colored labor gang No. 9' who did not exist. Gravier supplied the names (lifted from his hiring-hall lists, including men overseas and dead), his men collected the hundred and forty pay envelopes at the colored window every Friday, and Pruett, who was supposed to check the yard's labor against its gate counts, certified every voucher. About $640,000: Gravier kept a third, Pruett took $400 a week, and Lucien took the rest, more than $350,000, for his gambling debts, the house and the revival of the Krewe of Oneiros, of which he is the secret captain. Honoré never knew of gang No. 9. Marcel Fontenot, the paymaster's clerk, filled every envelope, both kinds, for three years and said nothing; he was paid a $25 weekly 'bonus' and was afraid. His wife Irene typed the Navy copies in the cost office until 1944. In January 1946 the yard laid off every Black welder without a dime of the spread; Marcel watched Theo Dorsainville's gang go out of the gate. The yard is being sold to Calumet Marine of Chicago, closing Thursday 7 March, on condition that the Navy settles the contracts, and the Navy's auditor, Lt. Pierce Whitcombe, is to sign a final settlement of $38,000 at noon on Ash Wednesday, which will close them against further claim. On Monday 25 February Marcel went to the Equity hall and told Theo he had the other half of the proof. On Tuesday 26 February he telephoned the Navy cost office asking for 'whoever is honest'; Chief Yeoman Albert Sallis, who has been Pruett's creature since 1943, passed the message to Pruett. On Wednesday 27 February Pruett telephoned Marcel, introduced himself as the Navy's former resident inspector 'who has wanted to put this right for three years', and asked to meet. That night Marcel took the Navy-copy pay summaries and the colored-window envelope register from the pay vault, pawned his watch for $20, had sixty-one pages photostatted at Crescent Photostat Co. on Carondelet Street, and at 10:50 p.m., using his night pass, went into the mold loft and pushed the originals, wrapped in oilcloth, under the third scale from the tail on the port side of the Leviathan, float fourteen of the Krewe of Oneiros, which Anatole Pichon's men were finishing. On Thursday 28 February at 9 p.m. he met Pruett on the yard's fitting-out pier with the photostats in his briefcase. Pruett asked for the originals; Marcel, frightened by how much Pruett already knew, would not say where they were. Pruett hit him twice behind the left ear with a leather Navy shore-patrol sap, killing him, poured half a pint of rye over his coat, and rolled him off the pier, kept the photostats, and walked back to the mold loft, where he was helping dress the Leviathan, with wet trouser cuffs. At 10:45 he telephoned Lucien at the Oneiros club rooms: 'Your clerk won't be a problem. The papers are safe with me.'
controlFile.theCoverUp: Each Ste. Claire believes the other killed Marcel Fontenot, and each is covering for the other. Honoré: at 5:50 a.m. Friday Clovis Pinac, the night watchman, telephoned him that Fontenot's Plymouth was in the yard lot and that the gate log showed Lucien's Cadillac in that night too (Lucien was in the mold loft with the floats until a little after nine, and saw Pruett walk out toward the fitting-out pier with Marcel, and chose not to think about it). Honoré concluded that his son had had the clerk killed, and at 6:10 a.m., before anyone had told him there was a body, he telephoned Captain Achille Lebeau, who has taken his money for twenty years, and told him that if a man from the Ste. Claire yard turned up in the canal it would be an accident. He had Pinac drive the Plymouth out of the yard and park it on Jourdan Avenue, and tear the Thursday page out of the gate log. He has told no one, and says to Lebeau on Saturday, 'My son is a fool, Achille, not a murderer, and I will not see him tried for it.' Lucien: he heard his father's 6:10 call on the library extension, then Pinac's account of the car, and concluded that his father had found out about the clerk and had him killed by the yard's men. He took Pruett's 10:45 call to mean that Pruett had bought or frightened Marcel. He told Gravier on Saturday, 'I never told anyone to touch him, Emile. I told you to find the papers,' and sent Gravier's men to search the Fontenot house. Neither man has asked the other. Pruett, who holds the photostats, means to sell them to Lucien for $50,000 on Ash Wednesday morning and to see the originals destroyed.
suspects: Commander Thaddeus Pruett, USNR (retired), 54: the Navy's resident inspector at Ste. Claire 1942–45, now the yard's 'government relations consultant' at $800 a month, a member of the Krewe of Oneiros since 1944 and Whitcombe's trusted adviser. THE KILLER. Motive: exposure means federal prison for bribery and fraud against the government. Plan: find and burn the originals, keep the photostats as a $50,000 sale to Lucien, see the settlement signed at noon Wednesday and leave on the 1:15 Crescent Limited. Charming, patient, cold.

Lucien Ste. Claire, 47: president of the yard and secret captain of the Krewe of Oneiros. Ran gang No. 9. Did not order the killing, and believes his father did. Motive: ruin, prison and the end of the krewe he has spent stolen money to revive. Plan: get the papers back, close the sale, go to Havana. Weak, kind to his daughter, terrified.

Honoré Ste. Claire, 74: founder and chairman. Approved the helper-rate spread and believes it no crime. Did not order the killing, and believes his son did. Covered it up. Motive: the yard, the family name and his son. Plan: close the sale and keep his son out of prison. Formidable, courteous, utterly sure of his place in the world.

Emile Gravier, 52: stevedore contractor, Gravier Stevedoring, the Poland Avenue wharf. Supplied the ghost names and collected the envelopes. Did not kill Marcel. Motive: his third of $640,000, and the hiring hall he rules. Plan: search for the papers, burn the welders' envelopes at the Equity hall on Lundi Gras night, and frighten anyone asking. Use Waterfront Boss; his men are Dockside Goons and Street Toughs.

Captain Achille Lebeau, 58: 5th District, NOPD. Ruled the death an accident on Honoré's word before the coroner saw the body. Not a suspect in the killing but the cover-up's hand: he takes Marcel's notebook from the property room, puts Det. Lamarque on the parade detail, and arrests Theo Dorsainville on Ash Wednesday morning. Use Police Captain.

Irene Fontenot, 36: the widow, who hired the party. A red herring of the classic kind (she gains a $2,000 insurance policy if the death is ruled an accident and nothing if murder, under a clause excluding 'death while engaged in an unlawful act' which Vidrine will argue), but she is exactly what she seems: the woman who told her husband to do the right thing.
redHerrings: Irene Fontenot's insurance: the policy pays $2,000 on an accidental death, and a murder ruling would let the company argue Marcel was killed while stealing company property. She hired the party anyway, against her own interest, because she wants his name. If the party accuses her, she slaps the nearest one and then helps them.

Emile Gravier is the obvious murderer: his men are on the docks, he lent half the Ninth Ward money, and they search the Fontenot house. He did not do it, and when accused he is offended: 'I don't kill pay clerks. Pay clerks are how I get paid.' He is guilty of everything else.

Lucien Ste. Claire's car was in the yard on Thursday night, he was seen white-faced at the Café Isabeau at 11:30, and he has the strongest motive. He is guilty of the fraud and innocent of the murder, and his collapse when he learns who did it is the scene that breaks open the cover-up.

The grey car Zélie saw coming off Jourdan Avenue at 9:15 with its lights off was Lucien's Cadillac, driven by Lucien, leaving the yard after he saw Pruett walking out toward the fitting-out pier with Marcel. He did not see what happened and did not want to. It is real evidence that Lucien was there, and of nothing else.
clues: A1 (cs-scenario-001, morgue): no froth in the airways, no water in the lungs to speak of: dead before he went in. Core for any Doctor or a Forensics look; Dr. Toussaint finds it automatically.
A2 (cs-scenario-001, morgue): a depressed fracture behind the left ear, two blows, from something heavy, flexible and narrow, like a sap. Core.

A3 (cs-scenario-001, Fontenot house and coroner's file): rye soaked into the coat and none on the breath or in him; the deputy coroner did not take a blood or stomach sample; Irene says he had not had a drink since 1931.
A4 (cs-scenario-001, the lock): the lock tender, Fortuné Guidry: a drowned drunk floats for days; this one was in the water a few hours and his wallet still held $11 and his yard pass.
B1 (cs-scenario-001, morgue): red-lead primer and steel shot-blast grit in his hair and the seams of his coat: shipyard, a fitting-out pier where hulls are painted. Core.

B2 (cs-scenario-001, Jourdan Avenue and the yard gatehouse): his Plymouth parked on Jourdan Avenue outside the yard fence with the seat set for a taller man and yard gravel in the tread; the gate log's Thursday page is torn out, but its impression on the Friday page shows FONTENOT PLYM IN 20:40 and no OUT.

B3 (cs-scenario-001, the lock and the St. Claude bridge): Guidry's grandson, fishing off the levee, saw a flashlight on the Ste. Claire fitting-out pier at about 9:20 Thursday and heard a splash. Zélie Pichon (or the Tremé Taxi drivers) saw a long grey car come off Jourdan Avenue fast with its lights off at 9:15.
B4 (cs-scenario-001, Fontenot house): Irene: Marcel said he was going back to the yard at nine on Thursday 'to meet the Commander, who can make the Navy listen'.

C1 (cs-scenario-001, Fontenot house): Irene: on Wednesday he came home after midnight with paste and gold paint on his sleeve, frightened; he had pawned his watch; he had taken 'the Navy copies' from the vault.

C2 (cs-scenario-001, Crescent Photostat Co. and Ducros Loan Office): the pawn ticket for his watch ($20, Wednesday 27 February) and Mrs. Myrtle Hingle's memory: sixty-one pages of Navy pay forms photostatted Wednesday evening, paid in cash.
C3 (cs-scenario-001, Fontenot house): Gravier's men search the house Friday at 11 p.m.; someone is looking for papers.
C4 (cs-scenario-001, the agency office): Prosper Vidrine, attorney for the Ste. Claires, offers the party $500 on Saturday to recover 'company payroll records removed by the late Mr. Fontenot'.
D1 (cs-scenario-002, Equity hall): Theo Dorsainville's cigar box: three years of pay envelopes for sixty-one welders, every one stamped HELPER .78.

D2 (cs-scenario-002, yard office and later the Leviathan): the yard's own Navy-copy summaries (the originals, or the photostats once recovered) list the same men by name as Welder First Class, $1.20. Yvonne's thesis notes show the yard's State wage filings: 412 'colored helpers' and no Black welders at all.

D3 (cs-scenario-002, the yard's pay windows): Hippolyte 'Polo' Landry, the yard's messenger since 1919, carried the colored window's pay trays every Friday: a hundred and forty envelopes for gang No. 9 went every week to one of Gravier's men, and no one in that line ever met gang No. 9.

D4 (cs-scenario-002, Custom House cost office): Whitcombe's turnstile analysis: the yard billed about a hundred and forty more men per shift than passed its gates. Pruett's explanation, a night gang at the river gate: the river gate's padlock rusted shut in 1941.

D5 (cs-scenario-002, Statesman morgue and Theo's list): the names on gang No. 9 include Pvt. Alphonse Sylvain, killed when his transport was torpedoed in 1943, whose death the Statesman printed, and five other men who were overseas the whole war. Theo's 1944 copy of the gang No. 9 list confirms it.
E1 (cs-scenario-002, photostats, originals or Navy file): every padded voucher is certified 'T. W. Pruett, Comdr. USNR, Resident Inspector'.
E2 (cs-scenario-002, yard office): Pruett on the yard payroll since September 1945 as consultant, $800 a month, approved by Lucien.

E3 (cs-scenario-002, Custom House): Chief Yeoman Sallis's message pad: Tuesday 26 February, 'Man from St. C. yard, would not give name, wants whoever is honest, will call back Wed', with a pencilled 'T.P. advised'.
E4 (cs-scenario-002, Yvonne or the krewe programme): Pruett rides masked on float fourteen, the Leviathan; he asked on Monday to be moved to it. Everyone at the yard calls him 'the Commander'.

F1 (cs-scenario-002, 5th District property room): Marcel's pocket notebook, dried and stiff: last entries 'Cmdr — Thurs 9 — fitting-out pier' and 'Wed — Lev. 3rd scale fr. tail, port'. Lebeau takes it at 6 p.m. Monday.
F2 (cs-scenario-002, the mold loft): Anatole Pichon saw Marcel at the Leviathan at about 11 p.m. Wednesday with an oilcloth packet, and thought he was stealing gold leaf.
F3 (cs-scenario-002, the gatehouse): the night-pass log, Wednesday: FONTENOT IN 22:50 MOLD LOFT, OUT 23:20.
F4 (cs-scenario-001 or 002, Fontenot house): Irene: papier-mâché paste and gold paint on his sleeve on Wednesday night.
G1 (cs-scenario-003, Anatole Pichon or his men): Pruett left the mold loft at 8:45 Thursday night and came back at 10 with wet trouser cuffs and red lead on his shoes, and asked for a rag.

G2 (cs-scenario-004, Pruett's room 912 at the Hotel Vauclain and Alcée Toussaint): a leather Navy shore-patrol sap with brown dye that matches the smear on Marcel's shirt collar, which Alcée kept; Dr. Toussaint matches the seam to the wound.
G3 (cs-scenario-004, Terminal Station baggage room): Pruett's valise, checked Tuesday night, holds the photostats taken from Marcel's briefcase. Only the killer could have them.
G4 (cs-scenario-002/004, notebook and message pad): Marcel's 'Cmdr — Thurs 9' and Sallis's 'T.P. advised': Pruett arranged the meeting.
G5 (cs-scenario-003, the captain's room): Pruett to Lucien: 'Your father thinks you did it, Lucien. Let him.'
G6 (cs-scenario-004, the Esplanade house at 10 a.m.): Pruett: 'your son's clerk was the one problem I couldn't let him have'; Lucien: 'He killed Marcel Fontenot, Papa. On our pier.'
G7 (cs-scenario-004, the Custom House): Chief Yeoman Sallis gave Pruett Marcel's home telephone number on Wednesday 27 February.
H1 (cs-scenario-003/004, 5th District switchboard log or Det. Lamarque): Honoré Ste. Claire called Captain Lebeau at 6:10 a.m. Friday, before the body was identified.
H2 (cs-scenario-003/004, Clovis Pinac): the watchman moved Marcel's car at 6:30 a.m. Friday and tore out the log page on Honoré's order, and believes Lucien's people did the killing.
H3 (Yvonne, cs-scenario-002 onward): she heard both telephone calls on Saturday, Lucien to Gravier and Honoré to Lebeau.
H4 (cs-scenario-003, Solange or the Café Isabeau): Lucien, drunk, Thursday or Saturday: 'The old man always cleans up after me.'
J1 (cs-scenario-004, 5th District booking ledger): Theo Dorsainville booked for vagrancy in front of his own house, 'hold without bail until 1 p.m. per Capt.'
J2 (cs-scenario-004, switchboard log): Lebeau's 6:45 a.m. call to the Ste. Claire house, fifteen minutes before the arrest.
J3 (cs-scenario-004, the desk sergeant): 'I never booked one so somebody could miss an appointment.'

Fallback proof (cs-scenario-004, Crescent Photostat): Mrs. Hingle kept the negatives of Marcel's sixty-one sheets for thirty days; reprints take ninety minutes. Pruett does not know about them unless the party lets it slip.
controlFile.theMoralChoice: By Ash Wednesday morning the party can hold the originals, the welders' envelopes, Dr. Toussaint's findings and the names of Marcel's killer and his protectors. Everyone wants something different from the proof. Lt. Whitcombe wants the Navy's money back: with the originals he refuses to sign and refers the fraud to the U.S. Attorney, which sinks the sale, puts the yard into receivership and Lucien, Gravier and Pruett into federal court; the welders' wages become a creditor's claim that will take years, if it is ever paid. Theo Dorsainville wants the wages: Honoré will pay the sixty-one $187,000 in cash on Ash Wednesday, and put a clause rating Black welders as welders into the Calumet sale, if the party gives Whitcombe only the gang No. 9 papers (which ruin Lucien and Pruett) and keeps the helper-rate pages out of it, which saves Honoré and the sale. Octave wants the whole story printed, and Dr. Toussaint wants the coroner's practice exposed, which only a murder charge forces. Irene wants Marcel's name, which means saying publicly that he was murdered for doing right. Yvonne must choose between her grandfather and the truth, and can testify. The party also has to decide who arrests Pruett: Captain Lebeau will not, the Orleans Parish DA will not move against the Ste. Claires' friend without a confession, the Navy cannot charge a civilian with murder, and Det. Lamarque can, at the cost of his badge. There is no clean ending. Let the players argue, and let every companion argue with them.
outcomes: If the party gives everything to Whitcombe and the Statesman: the settlement is refused, the sale collapses, Pruett is arrested (by Lamarque, or by the FBI for the fraud), Lucien is indicted and flees or is taken, Honoré survives but the yard does not. The Statesman's story runs; the Times-Picayune prints a paragraph. The welders' claim is still in court in 1949. Marcel's death is reopened. Dr. Toussaint's forty-one cases are read into the record of a grand jury that does nothing with them, and are reprinted in every Black paper in the South.

If the party takes Honoré's deal: the welders are paid in cash at the Equity hall on Ash Wednesday evening, and the re-rating clause goes into the sale. Lucien and Pruett go down for gang No. 9 alone. Honoré keeps his name and his yard money. Octave may refuse to forgive it; Theo may call it the best day of his life and the worst. Nobody prints the helper-rate story.

If the party lets the papers burn or sells them: the settlement is signed, the yard is sold, Pruett leaves on the Crescent Limited with $50,000, Theo is in jail, Marcel is a drunk who fell in the canal, and the party is $500 richer. Make sure they know what they bought.

If Pruett is cornered at Terminal Station or the Custom House he will try to shoot his way out once, then surrender to an officer in uniform: he would rather be a fraud before a federal court than a murderer before an Orleans Parish jury.

Yvonne's choice can turn any ending: if she testifies to the two telephone calls, the cover-up is proven and Lebeau falls; if she tells her grandfather everything first, he may save his son by sacrificing himself, which is the most surprising and the most Ste. Claire thing he could do.
